..(Thursday night through Tuesday)
Issued at 353 AM EDT WED SEP 2 2026

As the long term period opens, the axis of an anomalously strong 500 
mb ridge will have shifted south and extend from the Carolinas to 
western KY, centered over the vicinity of the Southern Appalachians. 
By Friday, a 500 mb trough is expected to extend across eastern 
sections of the Great Lakes to the mid Atlantic states from a closed 
upper level low over Quebec. Multiple shortwaves are progged to be 
moving in northwest flow across the Great Lakes to Mid Atlantic at 
that time. The upper ridge should be at least temporarily less 
amplified at that point, with the ridge becoming centered further 
west in the mid MS Valley vicinity and Plains by Friday into Friday 
night. This will all occur downstream of an upper low in the 
vicinity of the Pacific Northwest and trough in the western 
Conus. 

Temperatures on Friday should still be hot, owing to continued 
influence from this ridge; however, highs should trend cooler 
compared to midweek as the forecast area finds itself more on the 
periphery of this ridging rather than being directly beneath it. In 
terms of sensible weather impacts, there is high confidence that 
temperatures will be firmly above average by around 10 degrees or 
so; thus, the main forecast question during this period is just how 
hot it will get on Friday before potential convective development. 
Deterministic guidance is generally split into two camps in this 
regard: either dew points are lower with a higher air temperature 
(GFS and MEX), or dewpoints are higher with a lower air temperature 
(ECMWF and ECX). The drier solutions have proven unrepresentative in 
this pattern thus far and too warm by several degrees, largely 
because of unrealistically deep mixing. Given this bias, it seems 
more likely that a cooler and higher dewpoint solution would 
continue from the near term into the day on Friday, with the NBM 
deterministic highs offering a reasonable middle ground. In support 
of this, the flow between the ridge of surface high pressure just 
south of the forecast area and a cold front associated with the 
upper low in Canada and troughing into the eastern Great Lakes 
sagging toward the Lower OH Valley region and mid Atlantic should 
promote southwesterly to westerly winds across the forecast area, 
maintaining these higher dewpoints. Meanwhile, dewpoints were 
largely maintained, expected to be generally in the upper 60s to 
lower 70s across the region. This will keep apparent temperatures 
generally just below heat advisory criteria, but triple digit heat 
indices are still anticipated at least briefly though convective 
development on Friday should provide relief at least in some areas. 
Preceding the day on Friday, relief will be relatively limited; 
clear skies and high pressure will allow for a modest ridge-valley 
split, but low temperatures will still generally fall into the low 
70s on ridges and the upper 60s in valleys (where typical fog 
formation is expected). 

By the weekend, the axis and base of the upper level trough will be 
to our east and southeast, with amplifying ridging west of the 
forecast area over the Great Plains. This pattern will place eastern 
Kentucky in a northwest flow regime aloft. At least a slight chance 
of showers and storms remain for Friday night as the cold front sags 
into the area. Chances for convection likely peak on Saturday, 
mainly in the scattered range, in conjunction with cold front 
continuing to sag south and southwest and the potential for multiple 
shortwaves embedded within this northwesterly flow. As is typical in 
these patterns, model spread and uncertainty remain quite high, 
particularly in regard to the timing of these features for Friday 
night to Saturday; accordingly, NBM PoPs remain quite broad brushed 
for now, with small chances lingering into Sunday, representing the 
averaging of numerous different timing solutions.

Thus, as timing and presence of individual waves becomes more 
certain, PoPs will bear some refining later to end the week. This 
northwest flow pattern will allow temperatures to return closer to 
normal, with highs mainly in the mid to upper 80s expected for 
Sunday and continuing into Tuesday. Ridging also looks to build back 
toward our area early next week, which results in diminishing pops 
by Monday and Tuesday and potentially more confined to the VA 
border.
